strengths: Addresses a practically important problem of LRM inefficiency with clear motivation and strong empirical results (35% cost reduction without performance loss)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 6 math datasets with thorough ablation studies demonstrating component effectiveness
Well-motivated combination of complementary techniques (reflection model for efficiency, reflection reward for performance preservation) with clear analysis of their distinct contributions
Insightful analysis showing overthinking is problem-specific (higher on easy problems, lower on hard problems) with principled mitigation strategy
Clear presentation of methodology with detailed experimental setup, hyperparameters, and prompts supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Evaluation scope severely limited to single distilled 7B model with no validation on larger models, from-scratch pretrained models, or non-math domains, raising significant generalization concerns
Dependency on external 32B LLM (Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct) for initial overthinking detection creates practical limitations and undermines efficiency claims

Overthinking detection and reflection reward rely on simplistic heuristics (keyword matching, gold answer requirement) with no comparison to alternative approaches; keywords may appear in non-reflective contexts
Experimental setup bias: training data filtered to only questions answerable in 4 samples (40k→30k); GRPO RLen baseline performs suspiciously poorly, raising hyperparameter fairness questions

Limited novelty in individual components (LLM-based detection, keyword rewards, sequential revision are each relatively standard); contribution is primarily in combination which is somewhat incremental
No error analysis or qualitative comparison of reasoning patterns; reflection reward based on keyword density cannot fully capture complex reflection phenomenon
Computational overhead (~10% additional cost) and reliance on reflection model during inference not fully quantified; training requires significant GPU resources (3× A800 80G for 120 hours)
Missing experiments on generalization: different model scales/architectures, non-math reasoning domains, and applicability without 32B external model during training

Complementary dual approach (reflection model + reflection reward) that targets distinct dimensions of the problem
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 6 math datasets with thorough ablations and analysis of reflection patterns across problem difficulties
Strong empirical results: 35% token reduction without performance loss under sufficient budget (16k)
Thoughtful technical design including clever overthinking detection via first-correct-answer identification
Honest discussion of limitations and good reproducibility (detailed prompts, experimental setup, promised code)

Critical unresolved dependency: entire training data generation requires running 32B Qwen model for overthinking detection, undermining efficiency motivation and scalability
Limited technical novelty: combines established techniques (length rewards, sequential revision, keyword-based detection) without theoretical insights or analysis of why combination works
Weak performance under realistic constrained budgets: <0.5% accuracy gain at 8k tokens where efficiency matters most; 35% improvement headline requires 16k budget
Reflection reward is ad-hoc and domain-specific: keyword set lacks justification, likely tuned for math, D₀.₂ threshold unexplained; unlikely to transfer to non-math reasoning tasks
Incomplete analysis of failure modes and when reflection model makes mistakes; online vs. offline comparison lacks depth despite RPO sometimes outperforming on 8k budget
Computational overhead (~10% training cost, need to train additional 7B model) partially offsets inference gains; 120 vs. 80 hour training time
Hyperparameter selection underspecified: many design choices (keywords, truncation strategies, quantiles) with limited sensitivity analysis beyond narrow ablations

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing practical efficiency needs of Large Reasoning Models, clearly demonstrated with concrete examples (Figure 1)

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 6 diverse math datasets with detailed ablations, comparisons to multiple baselines, and analysis of how the method preserves reflection ability on hard problems while reducing it on easy ones
Strong empirical results achieving 35% response shortening without performance degradation, with good balance between efficiency and accuracy maintenance
Thoughtful system design that handles edge cases (e.g., when revision makes correct answers incorrect) and provides multiple revision strategies with clear analysis of trade-offs
Clear presentation and good reproducibility with detailed experimental setup, promised code release, and comprehensive analysis of training dynamics and reflection density
weaknesses: Severely limited evaluation scope: only math benchmarks (no code, logical reasoning, commonsense); only 7B distilled models (no larger or from-scratch models), significantly limiting generalizability claims

Methodological concerns with core overthinking detection: heuristic definition based on answer presence in chunks, dependency on external Qwen2.5-32B model, acknowledged inability to guarantee complete elimination of overthinking, and lack of error analysis on detection accuracy

Limited novelty in individual components: detection is straightforward, reflection reward is simple keyword density metric, length reward follows prior work [46]; main novelty is combining these in online RL which is relatively incremental

Inadequate analysis of design choices: 50% token removal limit appears arbitrary without justification, reflection keywords appear manually selected without ablation, chunk splitting strategy unablated, D₀.₂ quantile shows sensitivity (Table 5) but no principled selection guidance
Training efficiency trade-offs not fully acknowledged: sequential revision adds ~10% computational cost that offsets some inference gains, making efficiency claims somewhat overstated
Insufficient statistical rigor: no error bars or confidence intervals despite high variance on small test sets (Amc23/Aime24: 8 samples each with ≥5% variance); significance of improvements unclear

Incomplete comparisons with concurrent work: many recent papers (L1, GRPO-LEAD, DAST, etc.) cited but not directly compared; no head-to-head comparison with L1 which uses similar online RL length control

Limited analysis of failure modes and design sensitivity: no discussion of when method fails, why fixed truncation fails so dramatically, error analysis on wrong predictions, or ablation of reflection keywords and chunk splitting choices

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing practical overthinking efficiency in LRMs with clear motivation (Figure 1)
Thorough experimental evaluation across 5 math datasets with extensive baselines and 8k/16k budgets
Strong empirical results: 36% token reduction without accuracy degradation, with good analysis of how reflection is preserved on hard problems
Comprehensive ablation studies validating both reflection model and reward components
Good insights on training dynamics and appropriate reflection frequency adaptation across problem difficulties
Reproducibility: detailed appendices with prompts, hyperparameters, and promised code release
Practical approach suitable for online deployment vs. expensive offline data generation
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: overthinking detection is straightforward (first correct answer), reflection model uses standard SFT, reflection reward uses simple keyword heuristics; contribution is primarily engineering combination
Significant practical overhead: requires training auxiliary 7B model (+50% training time), sequential revision causes parallelism bottlenecks (~10% additional cost), complex hyperparameter tuning

Scope limitations: main results restricted to math reasoning (5 datasets); general QA results (Appendix B.3) show modest improvements suggesting limited generalization; only validated on distilled 7B models, not pre-trained
Weak reflection detection: 32B distillation has 17% failure rate, answer-mention-based detection is noisy and language-specific, cannot 'guarantee complete elimination of overthinking'

Reflection reward design is heuristic-based and brittle: language-specific keywords ('wait', 'but', 'check', 'alternatively') may not capture all reflection types; quantile D₀.₂ selection lacks principled justification

Missing experimental rigor: no error bars/confidence intervals, no variance analysis across runs, small test sets (Aime24: 48 samples), GRPO RLen baseline shows suspicious ~6% accuracy collapse unexplained

strengths: Well-motivated practical problem with clear examples (Figure 1) demonstrating overthinking in LRMs
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 5 math datasets with difficulty variation and extensive ablations (Appendix B.4)
Solid analysis of reflection density patterns showing difficulty-dependent behavior (Table 4) and training dynamics (Figure 3)
Detailed cost analysis and reproducibility: promised code, comprehensive hyperparameters, prompts in appendix
Achieves meaningful practical result of 36% token reduction without accuracy loss on math benchmarks
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core components are established techniques (LLM prompting for detection, standard SFT distillation, keyword-based reward heuristics, GRPO + sequential revision), combined without deep innovation

Critical scope limitations: validated only on R1-7B distilled models, not pre-trained from scratch; authors explicitly avoid larger models due to computational cost; R1-1.5B results substantially weaker, suggesting limited generalization

Reflection model training has distribution mismatch: trained on correct responses only (74% of data usable) but applied to potentially incorrect paths during training; 17% failure rate in format compliance; only 1 epoch training

Oversimplified reflection reward: keyword-density approach ('wait', 'but', etc.) lacks principled design or theoretical justification; does not encourage genuine reflection, only penalizes below-threshold density

Experimental fairness concerns: baseline comparisons show suspicious degradation (GRPO RLen: 91.66%→85.97%); authors use published checkpoints rather than retraining baselines; combined method sometimes underperforms components (e.g., Table 2 shows MReflect degradation)
Weak generalization: results on general QA (Appendix B.3) show minimal improvements (~0.2-0.3% on MMLU-Pro); method appears specialized to math domain

Insufficient mechanistic analysis: why method maintains reflection on hard problems is post-hoc observation, not designed mechanism; claimed 'partial advantage' decomposition breaks when revision fails and samples are discarded

Overthinking detection fundamentally limited: requires explicit answer appearance in traces, gold answer during training, and chunking strategy; cannot handle problems where answers aren't explicitly stated

strengths: Strong empirical results: 36% response shortening without performance degradation across multiple math datasets with consistent improvements over baselines
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Multiple datasets of varying difficulty, extensive baseline comparisons, generalization to smaller models (1.5B) and general QA domains, thorough ablations

Insightful analysis: Detailed reflection ability analysis showing the method maintains reflection for hard problems while reducing it for easy ones; training dynamics analysis (Figure 3); transparency about costs and limitations
Well-motivated problem: Clear demonstration of overthinking issue in LRMs with concrete examples; practical importance for inference efficiency
Reproducibility: Code promised, detailed hyperparameters provided, all prompts included, hardware/runtime specifications reported
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Overthinking detection via LLM answer identification is straightforward; length/reflection rewards are incremental over prior work; main contribution is combination rather than novel components
Scope limitations: Primary evaluation on math domain (4/5 main datasets); only validated on distilled 7B model (R1-7B); not tested on LRMs pre-trained from scratch, limiting generalizability claims

Overthinking detection method practical limitations: Requires Qwen-32B model for detection (not universally available); computationally expensive two-step verification; cannot guarantee complete overthinking elimination; assumes explicit answer restatement
Heuristic reflection reward design: Uses hardcoded keywords ('wait', 'but', etc.); model and language-dependent; quantile threshold (0.2) lacks strong justification; limited transferability
Domain-specific reflection model training: Requires retraining for new domains (separate SFT for general QA); introduces ~10% computational overhead; standard distillation approach

Incomplete theoretical analysis: Equivalence to partial advantage argument (Section 4.2) is informal; limited justification for why the combination works; insufficient explanation of performance recovery dynamics
Training cost overhead: Requires 120h vs 80h baseline (50% overhead) on expensive hardware; sequential revision reduces parallelism, acknowledged but downplayed
Analysis gaps: Significant performance drops in some ablations (e.g., Table 2) not fully explained; sensitivity to detection quality not analyzed; limited failure case discussion
